lesson.title: Rebuilding Any Repeating Wave from Pure Tones
lesson.summary: The Fourier series is the mathematical statement that any periodic signal can be written as a sum of sine and cosine waves at the fundamental frequency and its harmonics, turning a wave's shape into a precise list of amplitudes and phases.
lesson.body:
For a periodic signal x(t) with period T and fundamental frequency f0 = 1/T, the Fourier series expresses it as x(t) = a0 + the sum, over n = 1 to infinity, of [an cos(2π n f0 t) + bn sin(2π n f0 t)]. Here a0 is the signal's DC, or average, value, and an and bn are the amplitudes of the cosine and sine components riding at each harmonic frequency n f0. Every periodic signal discussed in this chapter sequence, sine waves, square waves, triangle waves, sawtooth waves, digital clock signals, decomposes this way: a repeating waveform of any shape is, underneath, just a specific recipe of how much of each harmonic to add together.

The ideal square wave gives one of the cleanest worked examples in signal analysis. A square wave alternating between +1 V and -1 V, with fundamental frequency f0 = 1 kHz, has the known Fourier series x(t) = (4/π) times the sum over odd n of (1/n) sin(2π n f0 t). Compute the amplitudes of the first three nonzero terms directly. The fundamental term, n = 1, has amplitude (4/π)(1/1) = 4 / 3.14159 = 1.2732 V, at 1 kHz. The third-harmonic term, n = 3, has amplitude (4/π)(1/3) = 1.2732 / 3 = 0.4244 V, at 3 kHz. The fifth-harmonic term, n = 5, has amplitude (4/π)(1/5) = 1.2732 / 5 = 0.2546 V, at 5 kHz. Notice there is no term at all at 2 kHz or 4 kHz, consistent with the previous chapter's rule that an ideal square wave contains only odd harmonics.

Adding just these three sine waves together, 1.2732 V at 1 kHz, plus 0.4244 V at 3 kHz, plus 0.2546 V at 5 kHz, already produces a lumpy waveform that visibly leans toward the square wave's flat tops and steep transitions, complete with some ripple. Keep adding more odd harmonics, the 7th, 9th, and beyond, each with amplitude 4/(nπ) at frequency n f0, and the corners sharpen further. In the limit of infinitely many terms, the sum converges to the true square wave everywhere except exactly at the sharp jumps, where the partial sums always overshoot by a fixed percentage no matter how many terms are included, a well documented behavior known as the Gibbs phenomenon.

This closes the loop back to the very first chapters in this sequence. Op-amp bandwidth and slew rate only matter as much as they do because most real signals are not pure sine waves. An amplifier only needs to pass the fundamental frequency to reproduce a sine wave cleanly, but reproducing a square wave's sharp edges requires passing many of its harmonics too, each one demanding more bandwidth, and because those harmonics are what create the fast transitions at each edge, they can trigger slew-rate limiting even when the fundamental frequency alone looks comfortably within the amplifier's rated specs.
